Cheat sheet

CIIP Memorization Sheet

Print this and keep it beside you. The CIIP exam rewards recall of the DICOM and HL7 essentials, the IHE profiles and coding systems, the data-integrity checks that keep the right images with the right patient, the storage, network, and capacity arithmetic, the resilience and security rules, and the documents that run an imaging operation. Every name and number on this sheet is fair game.

Download the PDF Start the free course

1. The exam itself2. DICOM, HL7, IHE, and the codes3. Modalities, ancillary services, and display QC4. Image management5. Storage, networks, hardware, identity, data6. Systems management7. Operations8. Procurement and project management9. Communications and training10. Acronyms

01The exam itself

FactValue
Certifying bodyThe American Board of Imaging Informatics (ABII)
CredentialCertified Imaging Informatics Professional (CIIP), for the people who run imaging systems
Questions170 in all: 130 scored and 40 unscored pilot items. You cannot tell which are which
Time170 minutes (2 hours 50 minutes), plus 20 more for the tutorial, the non-disclosure agreement, and the survey
Question typesMostly single-best-answer multiple choice; some select-multiple (4 to 8 options), exhibit or video, and hot-area items
OrderQuestions appear in random order, not grouped by domain
Answer ruleYou must answer each question before the next one appears; you may flag it and come back
ToolsAn on-screen calculator is available
DeliveryA Pearson VUE test center or online with a remote proctor; any day, no testing windows
AttemptsThree attempts within 12 months of being found eligible; postponing does not move the 12 months
ScoreScaled 1 to 99; 75 passes. ABII states the scaled score is not a percentage. A preliminary result shows on screen
Fees$500 test; $250 retake; $250 re-application after a late cancel; $10 Pearson VUE reschedule fee
Cancel or rescheduleUp to one business day (24 hours) before a test-center appointment, or 30 minutes before an online one; later means reapplying
A missed appointmentForfeits the fee but does not count as one of the three attempts
Renewal24 continuing education credits every two years plus an annual renewal fee, with ten-year requirements on top
How the questions readInformatics scenarios that ask for the FIRST step, the MOST likely cause, or the BEST configuration, document, or recommendation
DomainScored questions (of 130)Questions in this course's 50-question tests
A. Procurement52
B. Project Management73
C. Operations166
D. Communications73
E. Training and Education52
F. Image Management239
G. Information Technology166
H. Systems Management208
I. Clinical Engineering135
J. Medical Imaging Informatics186
Eligibility category (seven points in all)Points and rules
TotalAt least 7 points, and every category minimum met
Experience (minimum 1, maximum 5)1 point per 12 months as a credentialed imaging professional, a healthcare IT professional, a healthcare informatics professional, or a non-certified radiologic technologist in the military
Academic education (minimum 0, maximum 5)Highest degree only, not cumulative: 1 for no degree but 30 semester credits (45 quarter); 2 for an associate degree of 60 semester credits; 3 for an associate degree of 90 semester credits; 4 for a bachelor's degree of 120 semester credits; 5 for a master's or doctorate
Imaging informatics degree1 extra point when the degree itself is in imaging informatics
Continuing education (minimum 1, maximum 4)1 point per 10 hours of imaging informatics continuing education taken within 18 months of applying
AccreditationThe school must be accredited by a mechanism the United States Department of Education or the Council for Higher Education Accreditation recognizes, or an equivalent authority abroad
This course's official-format test uses 75 percent. ABII's 75 is a scaled score, not a percentage, so treat 75 percent as a target, not a prediction.

02DICOM, HL7, IHE, and the codes

DICOM termWhat to remember
Information modelPatient, then study, then series, then instance. One patient has many studies, a study has many series, a series has many images or other objects
UIDA globally unique identifier made of numbers and dots, up to 64 characters, built on a root the organization owns. Study, series, and SOP instance UIDs each name one thing and must never repeat for different objects
SOP classPairs a service with an object type, such as CT Image Storage. It is the abstract syntax a presentation context proposes
SOP instanceOne object of that class, such as a single CT slice, named by its SOP instance UID
SCU and SCPThe service class user asks and the service class provider answers. On a store, the modality is the SCU and PACS is the SCP
C-ECHOThe DICOM ping: proves the AE titles, address, and port match and an association opens. It does not prove images will flow
C-STOREPushes one object to a provider. Modalities and routers use it to send images to PACS
C-FINDQueries a provider at the patient, study, series, or image level and returns matching identifiers
C-MOVEAsks a provider to send matching objects to a named destination AE title, which the provider must have configured with an address and port
C-GETRetrieves objects back over the same association, so no destination entry is needed
Modality worklist (MWL)The modality queries the RIS or a broker for scheduled procedures, so demographics are not typed by hand
MPPSModality performed procedure step: the modality reports that an exam started, ended, or was discontinued, and which images it made
Storage commitmentThe modality asks PACS to take responsibility for stored objects; only after the commitment does the modality delete its local copy
AssociationThe opening handshake between two AEs: one proposes presentation contexts, the other accepts or rejects each one, data flows, then a release ends it
Presentation contextOne abstract syntax (a SOP class) plus the transfer syntaxes the requester can use for it
Transfer syntax negotiationThe two sides agree how the bytes are encoded and compressed. If no proposed syntax is acceptable, that context is rejected and the objects are not sent
Conformance statementThe vendor document listing the SOP classes, SCU and SCP roles, transfer syntaxes, and options a product supports. Read it before buying or connecting a device
DICOMDIRThe index file on portable media that lists the studies on the disc or drive
Transfer syntaxUID and behavior
Implicit VR little endian1.2.840.10008.1.2: the default every device must support; uncompressed
Explicit VR little endian1.2.840.10008.1.2.1: uncompressed, each element states its value representation
JPEG lossless1.2.840.10008.1.2.4.70: compressed with every pixel recoverable
JPEG 2000 lossless only1.2.840.10008.1.2.4.90: lossless wavelet compression
JPEG 20001.2.840.10008.1.2.4.91: may be lossy
JPEG baseline1.2.840.10008.1.2.4.50: lossy, for review copies
RLE lossless1.2.840.10008.1.2.5: run-length encoding, lossless
Verification SOP class1.2.840.10008.1.1: the class C-ECHO uses
DICOM tagAttribute
(0010,0010)Patient's name
(0010,0020)Patient ID
(0008,0050)Accession number: ties the images to the order
(0008,0060)Modality
(0020,000D)Study instance UID
(0028,0010) and (0028,0011)Rows and columns, the image matrix
(0028,0100)Bits allocated per pixel
DICOM standard partWhat it covers
Part 3Information object definitions: what each object contains
Part 4Service class specifications: store, query, retrieve, worklist
Part 5Data structures and encoding
Part 6The data dictionary and the UID registry
Part 7Message exchange
Part 8Network communication support
Part 14The grayscale standard display function
Part 15Security and system management profiles, including de-identification
Part 18Web services: QIDO-RS, WADO-RS, STOW-RS
DICOMweb serviceWhat it does
QIDO-RSQuery (QIDO): find studies, series, or instances over HTTP
WADO-RSRetrieve (WADO): fetch objects or rendered images over HTTP
STOW-RSStore (STOW): send objects to a server over HTTP
The configuration tripletRule
AE titleThe name of the application, up to 16 characters and case-sensitive. Each side must list the other's exact AE title
IP address or host nameWhere the other device answers. A host name needs working DNS
PortThe listening port. The registered DICOM ports are 104 and 11112; DICOM over TLS is registered on 2762
Unknown AE titleThe association is rejected: fix the title on the receiver's allowed list
Wrong port or service downThe connection is refused
A firewall dropping the trafficThe connection times out with no answer
Both directionsMost routes need entries on both devices: the sender needs the receiver's triplet and the receiver needs the sender's title
HL7 v2 termWhat to remember
Message structureA message is a set of segments, one per line, each ending in a carriage return; segments hold fields separated by a pipe, with components, repeats, and subcomponents set by the delimiters in the first segment
DelimitersPipe for fields, caret for components, tilde for repeats, backslash for escapes, ampersand for subcomponents
MSHMessage header: sending and receiving application and facility, date and time, message type, control ID, version
PIDPatient identification: the identifier list in PID-3, the name in PID-5, birth date, sex
PV1Patient visit: location, class, attending provider
ORCCommon order: order control and the placer and filler order numbers
OBRObservation request: the procedure ordered; the filler order number commonly carries the accession number
OBXObservation result: one line of result, such as a line of report text, in OBX-5
ADTAdmit, discharge, transfer: carries patient registration, updates, and merges from the registration system to RIS and PACS
ORM or OMIOrders: a new, changed, or cancelled imaging order from the order entry system to the RIS
ORUUnsolicited result: the report text and status from the reporting system to the EMR
SIUScheduling: appointments booked or changed
MDMMedical document management: transcribed or scanned documents and their status
ACKThe acknowledgment. AA means accepted, AE means application error, AR means rejected
MLLPThe framing that carries HL7 over TCP: a start byte (0x0B), the message, then 0x1C and a carriage return. There is no universal port; the registered hl7 port is 2575 and sites often choose their own
Interface engineReceives, routes, queues, and maps messages between systems. A stalled queue is the first place to look when orders or reports stop arriving
FHIR termWhat to remember
ResourcesSmall named building blocks of health data, each with its own address and a defined set of fields
RESTPlain HTTPS calls (get, post, put, delete) carrying JSON or XML
PatientThe person
ServiceRequestThe order, such as an imaging request
ImagingStudyDescribes a study, its series, and its instances, and points at the DICOM objects
DiagnosticReportThe report and its status
IHE profileWhat it fixes
SWF and SWF.bScheduled workflow: order, schedule, acquire, store, commit, and report with consistent data across systems
PIRPatient information reconciliation: fixes demographics when a patient is imaged before registration is complete, such as a trauma
CPIConsistent presentation of images: the same grayscale appearance on every display
KINKey image note: flags significant images with a comment
PDIPortable data for imaging: the format for studies on CD, DVD, or USB, with a DICOMDIR
XDS-I.bCross-enterprise document sharing for imaging: a registry lists documents, a repository holds them, and a manifest points to the images
IIDInvoke image display: opens the viewer on the right study from another application
REMRadiation exposure monitoring: sends dose records to a registry for tracking
ATNAAudit trail and node authentication: central audit logging and encrypted connections between trusted nodes
CTConsistent time: every system synchronizes its clock to one source so audit trails line up
Integration statementThe vendor's declaration of which IHE profiles and actors a product supports
Coding systemUsed for
ICDDiagnoses and reasons for the exam
CPTProcedures and billing
SNOMED CTClinical terms: findings, body structures, and procedures in a single hierarchy
LOINCObservations and orders, including many laboratory and imaging order names
RadLexThe radiology lexicon: imaging terms
RadLex PlaybookStandard names and codes for imaging procedures, used to map local procedure names to one set

03Modalities, ancillary services, and display QC

ModalityWhat it produces and typical object sizeWorkflow quirk
RadiographyProjection images. A computed radiography study is about 20 to 50 MB (average 30); a digital radiography study about 36 to 90 MB (average 54)Technologist checks the image, demographics, and laterality before sending; wrong-side or wrong-patient errors start here
FluoroscopyReal-time x-ray: often a few key images or a cine run. A digital fluoroscopy study averages about 20 MB (10 to 50)Typically only a subset of images is archived; check what was sent
Mammography and tomosynthesisA screening study of 4 images is about 197 MB uncompressed at 50 micron pixels; a diagnostic study of 6 images about 296 MB. A tomosynthesis exam runs roughly 450 MB to 3 GBHeavily regulated; needs specialty display; lossy copies cannot serve as the legal record
CTAxial slices of 512 x 512 pixels at 2 bytes each, 524,288 bytes per slice. About 60 slices (32 MB) for a single-detector study; a multi-slice study of about 500 images averages 262 MB (range 131 MB to 2.1 GB)Thin-slice reconstructions multiply storage and can overwhelm a router or a worklist
MRIMatrix often 256 x 256 at 2 bytes. A study of about 200 images averages 26 MB (11 to 131 MB)Many series per study; sequences vary by vendor, so sizes vary too
Ultrasound640 x 480 images, 3 bytes for color. About 30 images averages 9.2 MB (6.1 to 18.4); cine loops are multi-frame objectsScanner is often unscheduled and typed by hand; worklist use and correct patient entry matter
Nuclear medicine and PETNuclear medicine images are 256 x 256 at 2 bytes; about 10 images averages 1.3 MB (0.3 to 3.8). PET studies are fused with their CTThe patient is radioactive after the dose; PET and CT parts must stay matched
CardiologyEcho cine loops, cath lab angiography of about 15 MB a study, and waveform objects such as ECGOften a separate department system or archive that must be connected to the enterprise
Radiation therapyPlanning images plus plan, structure set, and dose objectsObjects are special DICOM types; the oncology system, not PACS alone, consumes them
Interventional radiology (IR)Fluoroscopy and angiography images, about 15 MB for an angiography studyProcedure room images and dose reports must reach the record
Visible lightPhotos and video from cameras, endoscopes, or microscopes, often as encapsulated or multi-frame objectsCaptured outside radiology workflows, so the order or patient link is often missing

Ancillary and specialty services

  • Oncology and tumor tracking across serial exams
  • Surgical planning from 3D reconstructions
  • 3D printing of anatomical models
  • Stereotactic and navigation systems
  • Intraoperative imaging
  • Point-of-care ultrasound
  • Wound and medical photography
  • Digital pathology and whole-slide images, which are very large objects
Display QC itemWhat to remember
GSDFThe DICOM grayscale standard display function (Part 14). It maps each pixel value to a luminance so equal steps look equally different on every calibrated display
Just noticeable differenceThe smallest luminance change the eye can see; the GSDF spaces its steps by this
AAPM TG18 and TG270AAPM task group reports on display quality. TG270 replaced TG18 and its test patterns can be used for the same checks
Acceptance testDone once when the display is installed, with the full set of patterns and measurements
Routine testDone on a schedule afterward, with simpler checks and a visual pattern
Who performs itA medical physicist or a trained, supported team. For mammography displays, a qualified medical physicist is required before clinical use
Ambient light20 to 40 lux recommended for image interpretation
Maximum luminanceAt least 250 cd/m2 for general grayscale displays, with 350 or more common for primary reads; mammography displays need more, about 420 to 450
Contrast ratioMaximum luminance divided by minimum: above 250 for a diagnostic display and above 100 for a clinical one
Contrast responseWithin 10 percent of the GSDF
Luminance uniformityMeasure the four corners and the center; they should not differ by more than 30 percent
Matching displaysThe centers of the monitors at one workstation should not differ by more than 10 percent
Pixel dropoutDark specks in a white field that stay put; compare with the manufacturer's allowed amount
Noise checkA low-contrast dot pattern viewed at 30 cm: on a primary diagnosis display all dots are found in three of four quadrants, on others in two of four
Internal photometer checkCompare the internal sensor to an external meter at acceptance and every 10,000 backlight hours
Bit depthAt least 8 bits of luminance resolution
Do not guess from a clean imageA display can drift out of calibration with no visible fault; the test pattern and meter are the evidence

Clinical awareness the exam assumes

  • Electrical hazards: do not open powered equipment, and report damaged cords
  • Ionizing radiation: x-ray, CT, fluoroscopy, and nuclear medicine need shielding and dose awareness
  • Radiopharmaceuticals: nuclear medicine patients are a source of radiation after injection
  • MRI zones: a strong magnetic field that never turns off, so no ferromagnetic items beyond the screening point
  • Infection control: hand hygiene and cleaning of shared keyboards and equipment
  • Biohazards: blood and body fluid precautions in procedure rooms
  • The sterile field: stay out of it unless gowned and invited
  • Ask the department safety officer before entering an unfamiliar room

04Image management

Reading room topicWhat to remember
ErgonomicsAdjustable chairs with lumbar support, desks with adjustable height, comfortable keyboards and mice, and monitors set at a comfortable height and angle to cut neck and eye strain
Ambient lightDim, even, and controllable at each work area; 20 to 40 lux for reading; avoid glare and reflections on screens
Room layoutWorkstations placed so no window or lamp reflects in a screen, with room to move and to consult
NoiseAbsorb it with panels and carpeting, and isolate dictation users from each other
Temperature and airMany computers warm a room, so plan airflow and cooling for each workstation
Monitor positioningMatched displays side by side with the same luminance and calibration
Human-computer interfaceThe integration of the EMR (also called the EHR), RIS, PACS, and the reporting tool; input devices such as mice, keyboards, and dictation microphones; display devices
Workflow termWhat to remember
Hanging protocol or display protocolThe rules that decide how images are arranged on the screen for a given exam type, so the radiologist does not rearrange each study
Read-readyThe state when all images and priors have arrived and the study is complete enough to be read
Postprocessing and 3DReformats, multiplanar views, and rendering built from the stored slices
Key images and annotationsSelected images and marks that point out what matters, stored as their own objects
Priors and relevant-prior rulesThe rules that fetch earlier exams of the same patient and body part for comparison
Teaching filesCases kept for education, which must be de-identified
Remote interpretationTeleradiology and telehealth reads from another site, which depend on bandwidth and a secure connection
Workflow optimizationRouting, worklists, and protocol rules that put the right study in front of the right reader
Compression topicWhat to remember
LosslessEvery pixel is recovered exactly. Typical reduction is about 1.8 to 2.8 times, and storage planners often use 2.5 to 1
LossySome data is permanently discarded. Typical ratios used when interpreting are about 20 to 1 for radiography, 10 to 1 for CT, and 5 to 1 for MRI
Who decidesThe radiology department and its policies choose what may be lossy-compressed for interpretation; it is not a decision for IT alone
The ratio on the imageA lossy ratio must be stated on each image of the study
Lossy for reviewFits web distribution and review copies better than primary interpretation
Never lossy under local policyMammography images kept as the legal record; lossy compressed mammograms cannot serve as the legal record
The size formulaCompressed size equals original size divided by the ratio
Data integrity checkWhat it catches
Technologist exam QCImage count in PACS matches what was acquired; demographics, laterality, and procedure are right
Order reconciliationMatches each study to its order using the accession number
Storage commitmentConfirms PACS accepted responsibility before the modality deletes its copy
Modality worklistPrevents typing errors by pulling demographics from the RIS
MergeCombines two records created for one patient, usually by correcting the ID
SplitSeparates one record that holds two patients
MoveRelocates a series or study to the correct patient
The unverified or broken study queueHolds studies that cannot match an order or patient; someone must own and empty it daily
Audit of every correctionEvery merge, split, and move is logged with who and why
Report statusMeaning
PreliminaryAn early read, not yet signed as final
FinalThe signed report of record
AddendedA final report with an added note; the original text stays
CorrectedA final report replaced because of an error, flagged so readers know
Structured reportStandard fields and terms, easier to search and count
Narrative reportFree text, flexible but harder to analyze
Research and sharingWhat to remember
De-identificationRemove the 18 identifier types the HIPAA Safe Harbor method lists: names, locations smaller than a state, dates, and ID numbers, among others
Identifiers in an image filePatient name, ID, birth date, accession number, institution, physician names, and private tags
Burned-in annotationsText drawn into the pixels survives header cleaning and needs pixel-level removal
Face reconstructionsHead CT and MRI volumes can be rendered into a recognizable face
PseudonymizationReplaces identifiers with a code and keeps a separate key, so the link can be restored by those allowed
UIDsReplace them consistently so a study keeps its own structure without exposing the original
Teaching filesDe-identify before saving or sharing
Image exchangeWhat to remember
CD importLoad the disc, reconcile demographics to the right patient and order, and fix mismatches before the study joins the archive
PDI mediaStandard layout with a DICOMDIR; a viewer is often included
Cloud image exchangeSharing through a network service, usually with the sender pushing or the receiver pulling a study by link or query
XDS-I.bA standard way for enterprises to publish and fetch imaging documents
Export rulesPolicy decides who may export, what is exported, and how it is logged and tracked
Imported study riskWrong demographics, duplicate UIDs, unknown transfer syntaxes, and corrupt files

Archive retention

  • Retention varies by state, country, and type of record
  • Minors are often kept longer, until a set age past majority
  • Mammography: kept at least 5 years, or 10 years when the patient has no later mammogram at the facility, and longer if a state requires it
  • A policy owner, not IT alone, sets the schedule
  • Deletion happens only under written policy and is documented
  • A legal hold suspends deletion of any record involved in a case
  • The original from which the diagnosis was made is the record that must be kept
  • A digitized film copy is not the original for legal retention

Enterprise imaging

  • Visible light images from clinics, wards, and operating rooms
  • Cardiology images and waveforms in the same archive
  • Encounter-based imaging tied to a visit rather than a radiology order
  • One viewer and one archive across departments
  • A vendor neutral archive and a universal viewer
  • Consistent patient identity across every department

05Storage, networks, hardware, identity, data

Storage termWhat to remember
DASDirect-attached storage: drives attached to one server; simple, not shared
NASNetwork-attached storage: shared files over the network using SMB, CIFS, or NFS
SANStorage area network: shared block storage over a dedicated fabric using Fibre Channel or iSCSI
SSDSolid-state drive: flash, no moving parts, very fast reads and low latency; used for the active tier and databases
Object storageData stored as objects with IDs and metadata, reached by an interface like S3; scales widely and fits long-term archives
Block, file, and objectBlock is raw volumes for databases and servers; file is folders and shares; object is flat keyed storage
iSCSIBlock storage over ordinary TCP and Ethernet
Fibre ChannelBlock storage over its own fast fabric
SATA and SCSIDrive interfaces; SATA for lower-cost drives, SCSI for enterprise storage
SMB and CIFSThe Windows file-sharing protocol
NFSThe Unix and Linux file-sharing protocol
S3The common object storage interface; cloud archives use it
Archive termWhat to remember
OnlineFast storage holding current and recent studies
NearlineSlower storage for older studies, still retrievable on demand
OfflineMedia taken out of the system, retrieved by hand
TieringMoves studies between tiers by age and use
IOPSInput and output operations per second: the number of reads and writes a storage system sustains; a database needs high IOPS
ReplicationCopying data to another system or site as it changes
MirroringWriting the same data to two drives or arrays at once
SnapshotA point-in-time view of a volume used to roll back quickly; it is not a backup on its own
Cloud storageRented capacity; check egress costs, retrieval time, and who holds the encryption keys
VNAA vendor neutral archive stores images in standard formats behind open interfaces so one archive serves many systems and a change of PACS does not mean a data migration
RAID levelUsable capacity and failure tolerance
RAID 0Striping: all n drives are usable and a single failure loses everything
RAID 1Mirroring: usable capacity is n divided by 2; survives one failure per mirror pair
RAID 5Striping with single parity: usable is (n minus 1) drives; at least 3 drives; survives one failure
RAID 6Striping with double parity: usable is (n minus 2) drives; at least 4 drives; survives two failures
RAID 10Mirrored pairs then striped: usable is n divided by 2; at least 4 drives; survives one failure per pair
Worked exampleEight 4 TB drives give 32 TB for RAID 0, 28 TB for RAID 5, 24 TB for RAID 6, and 16 TB for RAID 1 or RAID 10
RAID is not a backupIt survives a failed drive, not deleted files, corruption, a fire, or ransomware
Network termWhat to remember
OSI layer 7, applicationHTTP, DICOM, and HL7 messages
OSI layer 6, presentationEncoding and encryption, such as TLS
OSI layer 5, sessionStarts, keeps, and ends a conversation, such as a DICOM association or a remote desktop session
OSI layer 4, transportTCP and UDP, with port numbers
OSI layer 3, networkIP addresses and routers
OSI layer 2, data linkEthernet frames, MAC addresses, switches, and VLANs
OSI layer 1, physicalCables, fiber, and radio
TCPConnection-oriented and reliable, with acknowledgment and retransmission; DICOM, HL7, and HTTP use it
UDPConnectionless and fast with no delivery guarantee; used by DNS lookups, time, and logging
Hub, switch, router, gatewayA hub repeats everything; a switch forwards by MAC address; a router moves traffic between networks by IP address; a gateway translates between different protocols or networks
TrunkA link that carries several VLANs between switches
Cat 5e and Cat 6Copper cable: gigabit Ethernet to 100 meters; Cat 6 also does 10 gigabit over shorter runs
FiberLight through glass: longer distance, no electrical noise; multimode for short runs, single-mode for long
LAN and WANA local network in one site versus a network linking sites
VLANA logical network on shared switches, used to separate devices such as modalities from office computers
VPNAn encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network
DNSResolves names to IP addresses; many AE title and viewer problems are really DNS problems
ARPResolves an IP address to a MAC address on the local network
NATTranslates private addresses to a public one; a modality behind NAT may not be reachable for a C-MOVE
DHCPHands out addresses automatically; give modalities and servers fixed or reserved addresses
Firewall and TLSA firewall allows or blocks by rule; TLS encrypts a connection and proves the server's identity with a certificate
ServiceCommon port
DICOM104 or 11112 (registered); 2762 for DICOM over TLS
HL7 over MLLPSite-chosen; 2575 is the registered hl7 port
HTTP80
HTTPS443
SSH22
RDP3389
LDAP389
LDAPS636
DNS53
SNMP161 for polling, 162 for traps
Bits, bytes, and transfer timeRule
Bits and bytes1 byte is 8 bits. File sizes use bytes; link speeds use bits per second
Transfer timeTime in seconds equals size in bits divided by link speed in bits per second
Worked exampleA 262 MB multi-slice CT is about 262 x 8 = 2,096 megabits. On a 1 Gbps link (1,000 megabits per second) that is about 2.1 seconds at best; on a 100 Mbps link it is about 21 seconds
Real throughputAlways lower than the link speed because of protocol overhead, shared links, and slow disks; a plan should leave headroom
PrefixesKilo, mega, giga, and tera step by 1,000 for speeds; storage sellers use 1,000 and operating systems often report 1,024
Hardware termWhat to remember
CPURuns instructions; matters for servers, compression, and database queries
GPUGraphics processor; matters for 3D rendering and for the displays at a reading workstation
RAMWorking memory; a workstation viewing large studies needs plenty
DrivesSSD for speed and hard disks for capacity
NICNetwork interface card; a slow or duplex-mismatched one slows image loading
BusesPCI Express for cards, USB for peripherals, SCSI for drives
Server rolesDatabase, image archive, web viewer, interface engine, and application servers
Workstation rolesDiagnostic reading, clinical review, technologist QC, and administration
Software termWhat to remember
OSWindows, Linux, and mobile systems; versions must match what the vendor supports
RuntimesApplications often need a particular .NET or Java version
BrowserWeb viewers need a supported browser version
RDP and VNCRemote desktop tools; use them over a VPN and with access controls
VMA virtual machine: one physical server running several isolated servers
VDIVirtual desktop infrastructure: desktops hosted in the data center and shown remotely
Mobile devicesPhones and tablets need device management, encryption, and a lockable app
Identity termWhat to remember
Active DirectoryThe Microsoft directory holding users, groups, and computers
LDAP and LDAPSProtocol to query a directory; LDAPS is the encrypted version
Group policyPushes settings to computers and users from the directory
SSOSign in once to reach many applications; Kerberos does it inside a Windows domain
SAMLXML tokens that let an identity provider vouch for you to another application
OAuth 2.0Delegated authorization: an app gets a token to act for you without your password
Two-factor authenticationSomething you know plus something you have, such as a code on a phone
RBACRole-based access control: permissions attach to roles, and people hold roles
Data termWhat to remember
SELECTChooses the columns to return
WHEREFilters rows by a condition
JOINCombines rows from two tables on a matching key
GROUP BYGroups rows so a count or sum is computed per group
Primary keyA column that uniquely identifies a row, such as an accession number in an exam table
Foreign keyA column that points to another table's primary key
NormalizationSplitting data into related tables so each fact is stored once
IndexA structure that speeds up searches on a column; too many slow writes
SQLThe language used to query and change a relational database
CSVPlain text with comma-separated values; easy to export and open
XML and JSONStructured text formats for exchange; JSON is lighter
RTF and PDFFormatted document formats; RTF is editable, PDF is fixed for viewing

06Systems management

FormulaHow to use it
Study sizeImages x rows x columns x bytes per pixel. A 512 x 512 CT slice at 2 bytes is 524,288 bytes; 60 slices come to about 31.5 million bytes
Annual storageExams per year x average study size. Add imports, growth, and a second copy
Worked annual example100,000 general radiology studies a year need about 4.1 TB uncompressed: radiography 64 percent at 42 MB, CT 20 percent at 52 MB, MRI 5 percent at 39 MB, ultrasound 5 percent at 18 MB, nuclear medicine 3 percent at 1.3 MB, angiography 3 percent at 15 MB
Compressed sizeOriginal size divided by the ratio. A 4.1 TB year at 2.5 to 1 lossless is about 1.6 TB
Transfer timeSize in bits divided by link speed in bits per second
Downtime per year(1 minus availability) x 525,600 minutes
AvailabilityUptime divided by total time
AvailabilityDowntime allowed per year
99 percent5,256 minutes, about 87.6 hours
99.9 percent525.6 minutes, about 8.8 hours
99.99 percent52.56 minutes
99.999 percent5.256 minutes
Reading the numberEach extra nine cuts allowed downtime to a tenth and costs much more. Check whether planned maintenance counts
Licensing modelWhat it means
SubscriptionPay on a recurring basis; stops working or loses support if you stop paying
PerpetualPay once and own the license; support and upgrades are bought separately
EnterpriseOne license covers the whole organization
ConcurrentCounts how many people use it at the same time
Named userCounts specific people no matter when they log in
Per studyCost rises with exam volume
Testing termWhat to remember
Test strategyWhat will be tested, by whom, in what order, and what counts as a pass
EnvironmentA test system separate from production, with the same interfaces
Test dataFake or de-identified patients; never real data in a test system without the same protections
TestersA mix of administrators, technologists, and radiologists who do the real work
Unit testOne component works alone
Functional testA feature does what the specification says
Integration testTwo or more systems exchange data correctly
Workflow testA real scenario runs from order to report
Regression testOld features still work after a change
User acceptance testUsers confirm the system does their job; sign-off follows
Stress and scalability testBehavior under heavy load or growth
Security testWeak passwords, open ports, and access control checks
Test cases, scripts, suites, resultsA case is one check; a script is the steps; a suite is a group; the results are recorded for the sign-off
Resilience termWhat to remember
Redundant componentsDuplicates of parts such as power supplies, drives, and network cards
HAHigh availability: a design that keeps service running through a failure
ClusteringSeveral servers acting as one so another takes over
Load balancingSpreads requests across servers
Failover and failbackFailover moves service to the backup; failback returns it to the primary after repair
Synchronous replicationA write is not finished until both copies have it: no data loss, but it needs a fast link
Asynchronous replicationThe primary does not wait; the copy lags and a failure can lose the most recent data
RPORecovery point objective: how much data you can afford to lose, measured as time
RTORecovery time objective: how long you can be down before service must be back
BC and DRBusiness continuity keeps the work going while systems are down; disaster recovery restores the systems
Downtime proceduresWritten steps for paper, local copies, and re-entry
Downtime viewerA read-only copy of recent images and reports available when the main system is down
Monitoring termWhat to remember
Incident reportingA ticket system with a priority, owner, and a record of what was done
DashboardsA live view of the interface queues, storage, and server health
AlertsNotices on a threshold, such as storage at 80 percent or a stalled queue
SNMPA protocol for polling devices and receiving traps
Log aggregationCollecting logs in one place to search across systems
Protocol analysisCapturing network traffic to see exactly what was sent
DICOM simulators and validatorsTools that mimic a modality or PACS and check files and messages against the standard

Root cause analysis steps

  • 1. Define the problem
  • 2. Collect data
  • 3. Identify causal factors
  • 4. Find the root cause or causes
  • 5. Develop and implement the solution
  • 6. Write a status report and confirm the fix held
Migration termWhat to remember
ScopeWhich systems, years, and data types move
Push and pullPush: the old system sends; pull: the new one asks
Big-bang versus phasedEverything at one cutover, or in stages with parallel running
PrefetchLoading likely-needed priors onto the new system before cutover
Physical transferShipping drives when the network is too slow
Data cleanup and standardizationFixing patient IDs, names, and procedure names before or during the move
Proprietary data and conversionAnnotations, key images, and reports in a vendor format may need conversion or may not move
Validation and reconciliationCompare counts by patient, study, series, and image between old and new, and sample images
Cost and user impactPlan for temporary slowdowns, extra storage, and training
Progress reportsStudies moved, studies failed, and estimated completion
Security and privacyWhat to remember
HIPAA privacy ruleGoverns use and disclosure of protected health information
HIPAA security ruleRequires administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic information
HITECHExtends HIPAA and sets breach notification duties
GDPREuropean privacy regulation with strict consent and data-subject rights
PIPEDACanadian federal privacy law for private-sector organizations
Practice parameterThe joint ACR, AAPM, and SIIM document on electronic practice of medical imaging
NISTThe United States standards body whose frameworks guide security controls
Physical securityLocked server rooms, badge access, and screen privacy
System and network securityPatching, hardening, segmentation, and firewalls
Endpoint and application securityAntimalware, least privilege, and secure application settings
EncryptionAt rest on disks and backups, and in transit with TLS
Audit trailsRecord who opened which record and when; review them for snooping

07Operations

Quality improvement termWhat to remember
PhilosophyImprove the process, not blame the person; measure, change, and measure again
PDSAPlan, do, study, act: a small test of change repeated in cycles
Six Sigma DMAICDefine, measure, analyze, improve, control: a data-driven method to cut defects
LeanRemove waste such as waiting, extra steps, rework, and unused talent
SBARSituation, background, assessment, recommendation: a clear way to communicate a problem
Fishbone chartCause-and-effect diagram that groups possible causes
Pareto chartBars ranked by size; a few causes make most of the problem
Run chart and control chartA run chart shows a measure over time; a control chart adds limits to tell normal variation from a real change

Policies and procedures

  • Downtime policy
  • Incident management policy
  • Backup and recovery policy
  • Privacy and security policy
  • Access and role policy
  • Periodic account review and removal of leavers
  • User management: who gets which role, and how access is granted and removed
  • Written, approved, and reviewed on a schedule
Compliance topicWhat to remember
HIPAAPrivacy and security of protected health information
HITECHBreach notification and stronger enforcement
MQSAThe federal mammography law: facility accreditation, qualified reading physicians, and record keeping
Radiation dose trackingCollect dose data from each exam and compare it to reference levels

Change control

  • Request: who wants what and why
  • Impact review: systems, users, interfaces, and risk
  • Approval by a change board
  • Schedule in an agreed window
  • Back-out plan written before the change
  • Communication to affected users
  • Test and implement
  • Post-change review
KPIWhat it tells you
UptimePercent of time the system was available
Capacity used and remainingStorage and growth rate, giving months until full
Exceptions and broken studiesStudies stuck in verification, unmatched, or failed
Unread examsExams waiting past the target time
Lost studiesStudies sent but never found
Report turnaroundTime from exam complete to final report
Interface queue depthMessages waiting to be delivered; a growing queue means a stalled interface
ChartUse it for
Pivot tableSummarizing a long list by categories, such as exams by modality and month
Bar chartComparing amounts across categories
Line chartA trend over time
Scatter plotThe relationship between two measures
DashboardMany live measures on one screen for monitoring
Vendor documentWhat it states
SOWStatement of work: exactly what the vendor will deliver, when, and who does what
SMASupport and maintenance agreement: what is covered after go-live and what it costs
SLAService level agreement: response times, resolution times, and uptime guarantees, and what happens if missed
Response versus resolutionResponse is when they begin; resolution is when it is fixed
Contract renewalReview terms, price increases, and need before the date; auto-renewal can lock you in
EOSLEnd of service life: the date the vendor stops supporting the product, which forces an upgrade or replacement
Operational budgetThe recurring cost to run a system: support, licenses, storage growth, and staff

08Procurement and project management

Procurement stepWhat to remember
JustificationWhy the organization needs it, supported by total cost of ownership and return on investment
TCOEverything the system costs over its life: purchase, installation, licenses, hardware, storage, support, staff, training, and migration
ROIReturn on investment: (gain minus cost) divided by cost, as a percent. Spending 200,000 to gain 250,000 over five years is 25 percent
Payback periodInitial cost divided by annual net benefit. 200,000 divided by 50,000 a year is 4 years
Goals, scope, and budgetWritten down and agreed first; a preliminary budget comes before bids
Procurement policy and governanceThe organization's rules for buying and who decides
The planMilestones and dates for the whole selection
Needs assessmentCollect, document, analyze, prioritize, and validate requirements with the users
RFIRequest for information: learn who the vendors are and what they offer
RFPRequest for proposal: detailed requirements and a request for a full answer and price
RFQRequest for quotation: a price for a clearly defined item
Scripted demonstrationEvery vendor performs the same scenarios so they can be compared fairly
Reference calls and site visitsTalk to current customers of the same size and type
Scoring matrixWeighted criteria with scores for each vendor, filled in by all evaluators
SelectionPick on the scored evaluation and the references
Contract development and negotiationDefine deliverables, acceptance, support terms, price, and exit rights before signing
Project management termWhat to remember
Goals and scopeWhat the project will and will not do
Scope change controlEvery added request is reviewed for cost, time, and risk and approved or declined
RisksInternal ones come from within the project; external ones come from outside it
Risk registerA list of each risk, its likelihood, its impact, its owner, and its mitigation
DependenciesA task that cannot start until another finishes
WBSWork breakdown structure: the project split into smaller pieces of work
Resources and effort estimatesWho is needed and how many hours each task will take
MilestonesPoints that mark a major result
Critical pathThe longest chain of dependent tasks; a delay there delays the whole project
Gantt chartA timeline bar chart of tasks and dependencies
Time-and-task trackingRecording the real hours against the estimates
Status reportReports budget, schedule, resources, and quality on a regular basis
Go-liveThe cutover to production use
RetrospectiveA review of what went well and what did not
Lessons learnedWritten after go-live so the next project benefits

09Communications and training

RoleWhat they do
CMIOChief medical informatics officer: a physician who leads clinical systems use
CIOChief information officer: leads IT for the organization
Department chairLeads a clinical department
Section chiefLeads a subspecialty section within a department
AttendingThe senior physician responsible for the patient and the report
Resident and fellowPhysicians in training; residents are earlier in training than fellows
TechnologistPerforms the exam and checks its quality
PACS administratorRuns the imaging systems day to day
InformaticistDesigns workflows and connects clinical and technical staff

Settings and specialties

  • Ambulatory and outpatient clinics
  • Academic medical centers
  • Private practice groups
  • Pediatrics, with special sizes and protocols
  • Research sites and trials
  • Radiology, orthopedics, neurology, oncology, and cardiology
TerminologyWhat to remember
Anatomical planesAxial divides top from bottom, coronal divides front from back, sagittal divides left from right
Directional termsAnterior is front, posterior is back, superior is up, inferior is down, medial is toward the midline, lateral is away from it
ProjectionsAP: front to back; PA: back to front; lateral: side; oblique: at an angle
Body positionsSupine on the back, prone on the stomach, upright, decubitus lying on a side
LateralityRight or left side; getting it wrong is a serious data error
Modality-specific termsSlice, series, sequence, view, and phase mean different things in different modalities
Communicating a changeWhat to remember
WhoThe affected users and owners
WhatWhat is changing, and the effect on workflow
WhenThe start, the length, and the end
WhyThe reason, in the user's terms
HowWhat users must do differently, and who to call
By roleRadiologists, technologists, clerks, and clinicians need different messages
Notification channelsEmail, banner on the login screen, huddles, intranet, and phone for urgent cases
TimingGive notice early enough to plan, and send reminders before and after
Downtime and upgrade noticesState the duration, what to use meanwhile, and what to do when it ends

Strategic planning and feedback

  • Tie department goals to the organization's strategic plan
  • Use reporting tools to show progress against those goals
  • Collect feedback with surveys
  • Measure results and report them to leaders
  • Adjust the plan with what users say
Training termWhat to remember
Needs assessment triggersA new system, a workflow change, or a system upgrade
AudienceSize, location, and role decide the method
Instructional objectivesWhat the learner can do afterward, stated so it can be checked
Delivery settingsIn person or virtual
PresentationWritten guides, graphics, and video
E-learningSelf-paced modules that scale to a large audience
Super-usersTrained staff in each area who coach colleagues and report issues
AssessmentA quiz tests knowledge, observation checks the task, a survey gathers opinion
Task analysisBreak a job into steps to see where people fail

10Acronyms

Every acronym used in this course, 159 in all.

AcronymStands forMeaning
AAPMAmerican Association of Physicists in MedicineThe professional body whose task groups write the display and imaging quality control reports.
ABIIAmerican Board of Imaging InformaticsThe board that sets and awards the imaging informatics professional credential.
ACKAcknowledgmentThe HL7 reply message that tells the sender whether a message was received and accepted.
ACRAmerican College of RadiologyThe radiology professional society that publishes practice parameters and runs imaging accreditation programs.
ADTAdmit, Discharge, TransferThe HL7 message family that carries patient registration, updates, and merges.
AEApplication EntityA named DICOM endpoint; its AE title identifies the device or application on the network.
AGPAccelerated Graphics PortAn old graphics card slot you recognize on legacy workstations.
AIArtificial IntelligenceSoftware that learns patterns from data, used in imaging to flag or measure findings.
APAnteroposteriorA projection in which the x-ray beam enters the front of the body and exits the back.
ARPAddress Resolution ProtocolThe protocol that finds the hardware address that goes with an IP address on the local network.
ATNAAudit Trail and Node AuthenticationThe IHE profile for central audit logging and encrypted connections between trusted systems.
BCBusiness ContinuityThe plan for keeping clinical work going while systems are down.
CADComputer-Aided DetectionSoftware that marks areas on an image for the reader to consider, as a second look.
CDCompact DiscPortable media still used to hand a patient their images.
CIFSCommon Internet File SystemAn older name for the Windows file-sharing protocol.
CIIPCertified Imaging Informatics ProfessionalThe ABII credential for people who run imaging systems: 170 questions in 2 hours 50 minutes.
CIOChief Information OfficerThe executive who leads information technology for the organization.
CMIOChief Medical Informatics OfficerA physician leader who guides how clinical information systems are used.
CPIConsistent Presentation of ImagesThe IHE profile that makes grayscale images look the same on every display.
CPTCurrent Procedural TerminologyThe code set that names medical procedures for billing and reporting.
CPUCentral Processing UnitThe processor that runs a computer's instructions.
CSVComma-Separated ValuesA plain text file where each row is a record and commas separate the fields.
CTComputed TomographyImaging that builds cross-sectional slices from x-ray measurements.
DASDirect-Attached StorageDrives attached directly to one server and not shared over a storage network.
DHCPDynamic Host Configuration ProtocolThe service that hands out IP addresses and network settings automatically.
DICOMDigital Imaging and Communications in MedicineThe standard for image objects, the services that move them, and how devices connect.
DICOMDIRDICOM DirectoryThe index file on portable media that lists the studies on the disc or drive.
DMAICDefine, Measure, Analyze, Improve, ControlThe five phases of the Six Sigma improvement method.
DNSDomain Name SystemThe service that turns host names into IP addresses.
DRDisaster RecoveryThe plan and technology for restoring systems and data after a major failure.
DVDDigital Versatile DiscHigher-capacity optical media sometimes used for large studies.
DXADual-Energy X-ray AbsorptiometryThe bone density scan; its measurements can flow into the report as a structured report.
ECGElectrocardiogramA recording of the heart's electrical activity, stored in cardiology systems as a waveform.
EHRElectronic Health RecordThe shared digital record of a patient's care across providers and settings.
EMRElectronic Medical RecordThe digital record of a patient's care within one organization.
EOSLEnd of Service LifeThe date after which the vendor no longer supports a product.
FHIRFast Healthcare Interoperability ResourcesA web-based standard for exchanging health data as small resources over HTTPS.
FTPFile Transfer ProtocolAn older protocol for copying files between computers, with no encryption of its own.
GBGigabyteAbout one billion bytes; a large CT study can reach a few of them.
GDPRGeneral Data Protection RegulationThe European privacy law with strict consent and data-subject rights.
GPUGraphics Processing UnitThe processor that draws images and does 3D rendering.
GSDFGrayscale Standard Display FunctionThe DICOM curve that maps pixel values to luminance so equal steps look equal.
HAHigh AvailabilityA design that keeps a service running through the failure of a component.
HIPAAHealth Insurance Portability and Accountability ActThe United States law that protects health information and sets safeguards for its use.
HITECHHealth Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health ActThe law that strengthened HIPAA and added breach notification duties.
HL7Health Level SevenThe standard for messages that move orders, patient data, and reports between systems.
HTTPHypertext Transfer ProtocolThe protocol of the web, using port 80 by default.
HTTPSHypertext Transfer Protocol SecureHTTP carried inside TLS encryption, using port 443 by default.
ICDInternational Classification of DiseasesThe code set for diagnoses and reasons for care.
IDIdentifierA value that names one patient, order, or object.
IHEIntegrating the Healthcare EnterpriseThe initiative that defines profiles describing how standards are used together to solve a workflow problem.
IIDInvoke Image DisplayThe IHE profile that opens the viewer on the right study from another application.
IOPSInput/Output Operations Per SecondHow many reads and writes a storage system can sustain each second.
IPInternet ProtocolThe addressing protocol that moves packets between networks.
IRInterventional RadiologyImage-guided procedures done through small openings instead of surgery.
IRBInstitutional Review BoardThe committee that reviews research and says what patient data may leave the organization.
iSCSIInternet Small Computer System InterfaceBlock storage carried over ordinary TCP and Ethernet.
ITInformation TechnologyThe department and discipline that runs computers, networks, and servers.
JPEGJoint Photographic Experts GroupThe image compression family behind several DICOM transfer syntaxes.
JSONJavaScript Object NotationA lightweight text format for structured data, used by web services.
KINKey Image NoteThe IHE profile for flagging significant images with a comment.
KPIKey Performance IndicatorA measured number that shows how well a service is performing.
LANLocal Area NetworkA network inside one building or campus.
LDAPLightweight Directory Access ProtocolThe protocol for looking up users and groups in a directory, on port 389.
LDAPSLDAP over TLSThe encrypted form of LDAP, on port 636.
LOINCLogical Observation Identifiers Names and CodesThe code set for observations and orders, including many laboratory and imaging names.
MACMedia Access ControlThe hardware address of a network card, used by switches to forward frames.
MBMegabyteAbout one million bytes; a single CT slice is about half of one.
MDMMedical Document ManagementThe HL7 message family for transcribed or scanned documents and their status.
MLLPMinimal Lower Layer ProtocolThe simple framing that carries an HL7 message over a TCP connection.
MPPSModality Performed Procedure StepThe DICOM message in which a modality reports that an exam started, finished, or was stopped.
MQSAMammography Quality Standards ActThe United States law that regulates mammography facilities and records.
MRIMagnetic Resonance ImagingImaging that uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to make slices of the body.
MRNMedical Record NumberThe identifier a facility assigns to one patient across its systems.
MWLModality WorklistThe DICOM service that gives a modality its scheduled exams and demographics.
NASNetwork-Attached StorageShared file storage reached over the network with SMB or NFS.
NATNetwork Address TranslationA router function that maps private addresses to a public one.
NFSNetwork File SystemThe Unix and Linux protocol for sharing files over a network.
NICNetwork Interface CardThe hardware that connects a computer to the network.
NISTNational Institute of Standards and TechnologyThe United States standards body whose frameworks guide security controls.
OBXObservation Result SegmentThe HL7 segment that carries one result value, such as a line of report text.
OMIImaging Order MessageThe newer HL7 message type for imaging orders.
ORMOrder MessageThe HL7 message that carries a new, changed, or cancelled order.
ORUObservation Result UnsolicitedThe HL7 message that carries a report or result to the record.
OSOperating SystemThe base software that runs a computer, such as Windows or Linux.
OSIOpen Systems InterconnectionThe seven-layer model used to describe how network communication works.
PAPosteroanteriorA projection in which the x-ray beam enters the back of the body and exits the front.
PACSPicture Archiving and Communication SystemThe system that receives, stores, and displays medical images.
PCIPeripheral Component InterconnectThe expansion bus that connects cards such as graphics and network adapters.
PDFPortable Document FormatA fixed-layout document format used for reports and printouts.
PDIPortable Data for ImagingThe IHE profile for putting studies on CD, DVD, or USB in a standard layout.
PDSAPlan, Do, Study, ActA cycle for testing a small change and learning from the result.
PETPositron Emission TomographyNuclear imaging that shows how a tracer is used in the body.
PIDPatient Identification SegmentThe HL7 segment that carries the patient's identifiers and demographics.
PIPEDAPersonal Information Protection and Electronic Documents ActThe Canadian federal privacy law for private-sector organizations.
PIRPatient Information ReconciliationThe IHE profile that fixes demographics for patients imaged before registration is complete.
QAQuality AssuranceThe program of planned checks, records, and sign-offs that keeps a service within its limits.
QCQuality ControlChecks that confirm images, data, and equipment meet their standard.
QIDOQuery based on ID for DICOM ObjectsThe DICOMweb service that queries studies, series, and instances over HTTP.
RAIDRedundant Array of Independent DisksA way to combine drives for speed, redundancy, or both.
RAMRandom Access MemoryThe working memory a computer uses for running programs and data.
RBACRole-Based Access ControlPermissions are attached to roles, and people are given roles.
RDPRemote Desktop ProtocolThe Windows protocol for controlling a computer remotely, on port 3389.
REMRadiation Exposure MonitoringThe IHE profile that sends dose records to a registry for tracking.
RESTRepresentational State TransferA style of web service that uses plain HTTP requests to read and change resources.
RFIRequest for InformationA document asking vendors to describe what they offer.
RFPRequest for ProposalA formal document that states requirements and asks vendors for a full answer and price.
RFQRequest for QuotationA request for a price on a clearly defined item.
RISRadiology Information SystemThe system that schedules exams, tracks orders, and holds reports for radiology.
RLERun-Length EncodingA lossless compression that replaces repeats with a count and a value.
ROIReturn on InvestmentNet gain divided by cost, shown as a percent.
RPORecovery Point ObjectiveHow much recent data you can afford to lose, measured as time.
RTFRich Text FormatAn editable document format that keeps basic formatting.
RTORecovery Time ObjectiveHow long a service can be down before it must be back.
SAMLSecurity Assertion Markup LanguageXML tokens that let an identity provider vouch for a user to another application.
SANStorage Area NetworkA dedicated network that provides shared block storage to servers.
SATASerial Advanced Technology AttachmentA common drive connection for lower-cost disks and solid-state drives.
SBARSituation, Background, Assessment, RecommendationA short structure for communicating a problem clearly.
SCPService Class ProviderThe DICOM role that offers a service, such as the archive that accepts a store.
SCSISmall Computer System InterfaceA drive and device interface used in enterprise storage.
SCUService Class UserThe DICOM role that requests a service, such as a modality sending images.
SIIMSociety for Imaging Informatics in MedicineThe professional society for imaging informatics.
SIUScheduling Information UnsolicitedThe HL7 message family that carries appointment bookings and changes.
SLAService Level AgreementThe contract terms for response time, resolution time, and uptime.
SMASupport and Maintenance AgreementThe contract that covers support, fixes, and upgrades after go-live.
SMBServer Message BlockThe Windows file-sharing protocol.
SNMPSimple Network Management ProtocolThe protocol for polling devices and receiving alerts from them.
SNOMEDSystematized Nomenclature of MedicineThe large clinical terminology of findings, body structures, and procedures.
SOPService-Object PairA DICOM pairing of a service with an object type, such as CT Image Storage.
SOWStatement of WorkThe document that states exactly what a vendor will deliver and when.
SQLStructured Query LanguageThe language used to query and change a relational database.
SSDSolid-State DriveA flash storage drive with no moving parts.
SSHSecure ShellThe encrypted protocol for remote command-line access, on port 22.
SSOSingle Sign-OnOne login that gives access to many applications.
STOWStore Over the WebThe DICOMweb service that stores objects on a server over HTTP.
SWFScheduled WorkflowThe IHE profile for the order-to-report flow with consistent data across systems.
TBTerabyteAbout one trillion bytes, or 1,000 gigabytes.
TCOTotal Cost of OwnershipEverything a system costs over its life, not just the purchase price.
TCPTransmission Control ProtocolThe reliable, connection-oriented transport used by DICOM, HL7, and HTTP.
TG18Task Group 18The AAPM report that defined display test patterns and tolerances for diagnostic monitors.
TG270Task Group 270The AAPM report that replaced TG18 for display quality assurance.
TLSTransport Layer SecurityThe protocol that encrypts a connection and proves the server's identity.
UDPUser Datagram ProtocolA fast transport with no delivery guarantee.
UIDUnique IdentifierA globally unique dotted number that names a study, series, or object in DICOM.
URLUniform Resource LocatorA web address; a launch URL carries the patient and accession to open the right study.
USBUniversal Serial BusThe connection for peripherals and portable drives.
VDIVirtual Desktop InfrastructureDesktops that run in the data center and are shown on a user's screen.
VLANVirtual Local Area NetworkA logical network created on shared switches.
VMVirtual MachineA software-based server that shares physical hardware with others.
VNAVendor Neutral ArchiveAn archive that stores images in standard formats behind open interfaces.
VNCVirtual Network ComputingA remote desktop tool that shows another computer's screen.
VPNVirtual Private NetworkAn encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network.
VRValue RepresentationThe DICOM code that says what type of data an element holds.
VUEVirtual University EnterprisesThe name of the testing company that delivers the exam.
WADOWeb Access to DICOM ObjectsThe DICOMweb service that retrieves objects or rendered images over HTTP.
WANWide Area NetworkA network that links sites over long distances.
WBSWork Breakdown StructureThe project split into smaller pieces of work.
XDSCross-Enterprise Document SharingThe IHE approach to publishing and finding documents across organizations.
XMLExtensible Markup LanguageA structured text format that marks data with tags.
